title: ASOF JOIN memory usage
body: DuckDB runs out of memory while executing the `ASOF JOIN` query in `select_binance_transaction_times_and_prices.sql`. I provided an archive containing the scripts, SQL query, and transaction-time CSV needed to download and import the 2022 BTCUSDT trade history and reproduce the failure. I am using the DuckDB CLI, version v0.8.2-dev1764 07b0b0a2a4, on Ubuntu Server 22.04.

symptoms_visible: DuckDB runs out of memory while executing my BTCUSDT `ASOF JOIN` query.
N0.label: N0 ASOF JOIN out-of-memory report

symptoms_visible: On my 16 GB virtual machine, DuckDB creates `binance.duckdb.tmp` and fills it with many large files, but the query still runs out of memory and dies.
Setting `PRAGMA memory_limit="12GB"` does not prevent the failure.
N1.label: N1 spilling and memory limit measured

symptoms_visible: After converting price and quantity columns from `DOUBLE` to `DECIMAL`, `binance.duckdb` is about 25% smaller, but the `ASOF JOIN` runs out of disk space.
N2_x.label: N2_x decimal conversion aftermath

symptoms_visible: The `arg_max` rewrite completes in just under 21 seconds on my newer Ubuntu virtual machine, while the native `ASOF JOIN` remains the resource-heavy case.
N3.label: N3 arg_max workaround confirmed

symptoms_visible: Running an adapted version of my ASOF join query that instead uses a lateral join, DuckDB v1.1.2-dev38 unfortunately runs out of temporary disk space.
N3_lateral_x.label: N3_lateral_x lateral-join rewrite aftermath

symptoms_visible: With v1.3.0-dev1112, the original small-probe `ASOF JOIN` completes in just under 32 seconds even with a 45 MB memory limit.
When I expand the probe CSV to 240 rows, DuckDB quickly runs out of memory.
N4.label: N4 small-probe optimization has a scaling cutoff

symptoms_visible: With a 5 GB memory limit and the temporary directory set to the current directory, the 240-row probe query completes, but averages about 1611 seconds.
N5.label: N5 regular-plan paging behavior measured

symptoms_visible: With DuckDB v1.5.0-dev2458, the 240-row `ASOF JOIN` completes without an out-of-memory exception in about 88 seconds on average.
The original small-probe query still completes in about 32 seconds.
N_terminal.label: terminal ASOF memory issue resolved on 1.5 development build

question_patterns: How much memory is available, and does DuckDB spill to a configured temporary directory before it fails?
Please set or inspect `PRAGMA temp_directory` and report whether the query completes or still runs out of memory.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The virtual machine has 16 GB of memory. DuckDB already creates `binance.duckdb.tmp` and fills it with many large files, but it still runs out of memory and dies.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The query completes once I configure a temporary directory with enough free space, and memory stays below the machine limit.
The temporary files are created in a different directory, but the same 16 GB out-of-memory failure occurs.

edges.comment: The reporter checked the default spill directory after temporary-directory advice and later added that a 12 GB memory limit also failed. These are configuration measurements, not fixes.

solution.intent: Reduce the materialized and sorted row width by replacing the price and quantity `DOUBLE` columns with narrower `DECIMAL` types.
solution.concrete_example: Store price as `DECIMAL(10,2)`, quantity as `DECIMAL(12,8)`, and quote quantity as `DECIMAL(16,8)` instead of `DOUBLE`, then retry the native `ASOF JOIN`.

edges.comment: The narrower types reduced the database size by about 25%, but the native ASOF operation then exhausted available temporary disk space. This optimization alone was falsified as a complete fix.

solution.intent: Use an `arg_max` aggregation rewrite as a practical workaround for this query shape, placing the small transaction-time table on the inner side of a nested-loop inequality join.
solution.concrete_example: Join each transaction time to candidate prices satisfying `UTC_Time >= p.time`, then `GROUP BY UTC_Time` and return `arg_max(price, time)`. On this data the rewrite ran in roughly 32 seconds and about 8 GB in the engineer's test.
solution.inference_hint: The developer derived from the physical plan that the rewrite is effective because it becomes a nested-loop join with the small table on the inside. The reporter only supplied the observed runtime.

edges.comment: The reporter later confirmed that the supplied arg_max rewrite completed in just under 21 seconds. It is a successful workaround for the restricted query shape, not the eventual general ASOF implementation fix.

solution.intent: Install a current main build containing the alternate native ASOF plan for very small probe tables and retest the original query.
solution.concrete_example: Grab the latest development build containing the alternate ASOF plan. The planner selects a nested-loop strategy when the probe table is around 32–64 rows or smaller; the supplied case has roughly two dozen probe rows.
solution.inference_hint: That the arg_max rewrite works by becoming a nested-loop join with the small probe table on the inside is the engineer's own reading of the physical plan; the reporter reported only the runtime. The optimizer cutoff and choice of a native nested-loop ASOF plan are likewise implementation details supplied by the developer. The reporter's terminal-side observations are the 32-second success on the original input and failure after expanding the probe to 240 rows.

edges.comment: The first native optimization solved the original small-probe reproduction, even at a 45 MB limit, but did not scale to the reporter's later 240-row probe test.

question_patterns: With the 240-row probe input, can you set a finite memory limit and a temporary directory and report whether the regular plan completes and how long it takes?
Please benchmark the expanded probe table with enough spill space and share the raw runtime.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I set `memory_limit` to 5 GB and `temp_directory` to the directory where I ran the CLI. The 240-row query completed in an average of 1610.677 seconds.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The 240-row query completes in about the same 32 seconds as the original probe table and does not create substantial temporary data.
It completes with the same settings in about 1500 seconds instead of 1611 seconds.

edges.comment: This benchmark established the severe scaling and paging behavior above the small-probe nested-loop cutoff. The developer, not the reporter, concluded that the nested-loop plan becomes quadratic and that most regular-plan memory is spent sorting.

solution.intent: Upgrade to the latest DuckDB 1.5 development build containing the newer ASOF implementation, which reduces memory use and scans sorted data in parallel at finer granularity; verify both the original and expanded probe inputs before declaring the memory issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: Retest the native query on the latest 1.5 build. The updated regular ASOF path uses substantially more parallelism and lower-memory sort/scan processing; the developer's main-branch test completed at a 12 GB limit, and the reporter's v1.5.0-dev2458 test completed the 240-row probe in about 88 seconds without OOM.
solution.inference_hint: The root-cause interpretation comes from developer profiling: the old regular ASOF path uncompressed, copied, and sorted the large build side, while an inequality-only join effectively had a single partition and insufficient parallelism. Why the arg_max workaround was fast (a nested-loop join with the small probe table on the inside) is likewise an engineer plan reading, not a reporter observation. The reporter supplied runtimes and OOM behavior, then verified that v1.5.0-dev2458 no longer OOMed on the 240-row probe.

edges.comment: The reporter verified the final memory and performance improvement on v1.5.0-dev2458: about 88 seconds for 240 probe rows and about 32 seconds for the original input, with no OOM. A separately observed price-output discrepancy was redirected to a new targeted correctness issue and is outside this memory task.

solution.intent: Rewrite the `ASOF JOIN` as a `LATERAL` correlated subquery that picks the most recent price at or before each transaction time.
solution.concrete_example: Replace the join with `FROM "transaction_times.csv" t, LATERAL (SELECT price FROM prices p WHERE p.time <= t.UTC_Time ORDER BY p.time DESC LIMIT 1) p`, keeping the same 2022 date range filter.

edges.comment: The other obvious hand-rolled rewrite alongside `arg_max`, modelled on the TimescaleDB lateral-join formulation. The reporter actually executed it and reported that DuckDB v1.1.2-dev38 ran out of temporary disk space, so this direction was falsified in the thread.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the original resource cause: the regular ASOF implementation materialized, uncompressed, copied, and sorted the large price side, while the inequality-only case had limited parallelism; spilling or lowering `memory_limit` alone did not remove that cost.

Must distinguish the small-probe nested-loop optimization from the general fix: it works very well for the original roughly two-dozen-row probe but becomes impractical above its roughly 32–64-row cutoff, as demonstrated by the 240-row case.
Must not present conversion from `DOUBLE` to `DECIMAL` as the complete fix: it reduced database size by about 25%, but the native query still exhausted temporary disk space.

The `arg_max` rewrite may be offered as a successful workaround for this restricted query shape, but the native resolution is to move to a current build containing the reworked ASOF implementation, which uses less memory and scans the sorted data in parallel at a much finer granularity.
Diagnosis and recommendation must be grounded in the collected spill, memory-limit, small-probe, and 240-row benchmark results rather than inferred from the opening OOM alone.

Must ask the reporter to verify a build containing the ASOF changes and treat the memory issue as resolved only after the reporter confirms that both the original and 240-row probe queries complete without OOM.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically experienced database user comfortable with SQL rewrites, DuckDB pragmas, shell scripts, schema changes, development builds, virtual machines, and repeatable Hyperfine benchmarks.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, methodical, and cooperative; asks precise conceptual questions, reports exact versions and resource limits, supplies raw commands and benchmark output, and tests suggested changes on both the original and expanded workloads.
